1351:
History On February 25, Huang Jinhai phoned Geng Jinzhang and lured him to the No. 31 Mill. They shut the gates, pushed him onto a truck and took him to the Yangpu Public Security Sub-bureau. Wang Hongwen had told the sub-bureau beforehand, in the name of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee. Geng was held for more than two months and released on May 2. The same day Wang Hongwen held a meeting at the Jing'an District Cultural Center, declared Fan Zuodong a careerist, and had him taken to the Yangpu Public Security Sub-bureau. Fan was held for 24 days and released when questioning turned up nothing. Huang Wenhai was held for more than half a year. See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 9. The recollections of Ye Changming and Dai Liqing are attached in Ye's notes to that chapter, and their accounts differ slightly.

Disputed Huang Jinhai said that on the day Geng Jinzhang was lured and seized, “even Wang Hongwen didn't know how it would be done,” and that Wang Hongwen “was not actually there.” The second choice is a game branch. Huang Jinhai thought the arrest of Fan Zuodong “should not have happened, it was wrong.”

Fiction The second and third choices are game branches.
1353: Shanghai Diesel Engine Plant · People's Square
1355:
⟦0⟧

The Shanghai Diesel Engine Plant had split into two factions. The East Is Red had more Party members and more cadres, and it followed the Workers' General Headquarters. Liansi had more young people and more people who had been persecuted, and for a while it had run with the Scarlet Guards. The two factions fought inside the plant. The people from The East Is Red were beaten out of the gates and were afraid to come to work.

By spring, Liansi had moved out of the plant and into the city. A teaching assistant from Jiaotong University gave them ideas, and they set up the Support-Liansi Station. They said real power in the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee was not in the hands of the proletariat, and Shanghai needed a second great upheaval. They built a platform out of trucks in People's Square and brought a diesel generator from the plant. Every day someone went up to make speeches. People below who disagreed got beaten. ⟦1⟧

In January, Liansi locked the men the Yangpu liaison station had sent to investigate in an air-raid shelter. That night the liaison station sent more than a thousand people to block the plant gates. You rode over on a motorcycle with Chen Ada on the back seat. On Longchang Road you dozed off and the motorcycle went over. Chen Ada was thrown off, but he was all right. When you reached the plant gates, you told everyone not to move. You said this was not the time.

In mid-July, a Party branch secretary from one of the workshop sections of The East Is Red, a man called Xie Fuxi, was carried off by Liansi and beaten to death. The East Is Red people carried his body to the gates of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee and sat there. You went to look once. His face was so swollen you could not recognize it.

On July 31, Workers' General Headquarters men on Tai'an Road seized more than 30 leaders of the Support-Liansi Station in one sweep. They did not catch the Liansi leaders.
1356: Fan Zuodong was held for 24 days. Questioning turned up nothing, and he was sent back to the No. 2 Thermos Flask Factory.
1357: That night the meeting went on until midnight. Some said the notice was right. Some said Fan Zuodong just wanted to seize the seal. In the end there was a show of hands. Most said the Standing Committee members should keep office hours, and Fan Zuodong raised his hand too. The next day you sat at headquarters all day, and there were more phone calls than you could answer.
1358: At half past seven the next morning, you reached headquarters. Fan Zuodong had come in before you. Two cups of tea were brewing on the desk.
1359: You heard that some former Scarlet Guards often stood below the platform. They did not like Liansi, and they liked the Workers' General Headquarters even less.
1360: On the afternoon of August 3, you got a phone call. The trucks sent to Shanghai Diesel to spread propaganda had been smashed.

History The makeup of the two factions at Shanghai Diesel, The East Is Red and Liansi. Quan Xiangdong, a teaching assistant at Jiaotong University, started the Support-Liansi Station and built a platform in People's Square. Wang Hongwen crashed a motorcycle on Longchang Road with Chen Ada on the back, and when he arrived he said, “Don't move, this is not the time.” In mid-July Xie Fuxi, a workshop-section Party branch secretary, was kidnapped and beaten to death by Liansi, and there is an autopsy report. On July 31, more than 30 Support-Liansi Station leaders were seized on Tai'an Road. All from Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 9.

Ye Yonglie said Liansi once climbed the wall and broke into Zhang Chunqiao's house. Huang Jinhai said this never happened.
1365:
In the morning, the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee sent three propaganda trucks into Shanghai Diesel with an open letter to Liansi. All three trucks were smashed. The propaganda workers were beaten and their clothes torn. Their camera was taken, and several of them were locked in the air-raid shelter.

In the afternoon, everyone met at the Garrison Command Support-the-Left Office. The last three digits of its phone number were 888, so people called the place “888.” Xu Jingxian was there. Wang Chenglong from the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee office was there. Dai Liqing, Wang Feili and Ye Changming from the Workers' General Headquarters were all there. The Workers' General Headquarters men said the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee was too soft. Things had come this far, and it was still sending open letters. Wang Chenglong said only the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee could direct people and vehicles. The two sides started shouting. A few men got so angry they drove off. They parked at the Western Suburbs Park lot, vented for a while, and were talked into coming back.

After dark, the meeting moved to Kangping Road. Wang Shaoyong came too. On July 13, Zhang Chunqiao had said on the phone to keep a cool head, listen to both sides, calm things down, and not be afraid if there was some trouble. Everyone in the room was waiting for you to speak.

1368: August 3, 1967　Plotted a so-called denunciation rally to build public opinion for armed fighting.

History On the morning of August 3, the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee sent propaganda trucks to Shanghai Diesel to publicize the open letter. The trucks were smashed and people were beaten. That afternoon a meeting was held at the Garrison Command Support-the-Left Office, “888,” attended by Xu Jingxian, Wang Chenglong, Wang Hongwen, Dai Liqing, Wang Feili, Ye Changming, Zhang Baolin, Wang Minglong and others. The Workers' General Headquarters men quarreled with Wang Chenglong, and some drove to the Western Suburbs Park parking lot. In the evening the meeting moved to Kangping Road, with Wang Shaoyong also taking part, and they decided to hold a denunciation rally in People's Square that night. Zhang Chunqiao's phone instructions of July 13, “keep a cool head,” “listen to both sides,” “calm things down,” “don't be afraid if there is some trouble,” are recorded in “Ye Changming's Work Notes” (《叶昌明工作笔记》). See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 9, and Ye's notes.

Disputed Whether the rally was itself the mobilization to attack Liansi. Huang Jinhai and Ye Changming said the rally did not call on anyone to attack, and everyone went empty-handed. Ye Yonglie said Wang Hongwen had already laid out an “888 Plan” at “888” on July 29. Huang Jinhai said that was made up. The Special Court found that Wang Hongwen instigated and directed this armed fight. The second choice follows the account of the investigating side.

Fiction The third choice is a game branch.
1377: An office in a factory next to the Shanghai Diesel Engine Plant
1379:
Who Were the “Royalists”

After the power seizures of January, Party committees at every level were overthrown. What the conservatives had defended no longer existed, and “conservative” became another word for resisting the Cultural Revolution. No organization called itself conservative anymore. Labeling the opposing faction “royalists” and so stripping it of the right to take part in the movement became the most common way factions fought. At the Shanghai Diesel Engine Plant in the first half of 1967, Liansi and The East Is Red each called the other a “royalist organization,” and armed clashes never stopped. In fact both sides were rebel organizations. History See Li Xun, “Neglected History: Taking the Study of Cultural Revolution Conservatives Seriously” (《被忽略的历史：重视对文革保守派的研究》).

The standard for calling people “royalists” varied. Some looked at which side they had taken in 1966. Some looked at how many Party and Youth League members they had. Some looked at how close they were to the revolutionary committee and the Support the Left troops. Li Xun says that much of the time it was only an excuse to bring an opponent down. Interpretation

The Special Court verdict says Wang Hongwen “organized and directed the armed siege of the Shanghai Diesel Engine Plant, detaining and injuring or crippling 650 people.” Huang Jinhai says there were only two or three hundred Liansi members in the building. There is still no agreed figure for the casualties. Disputed

Wang Hongwen That Day

Drawing on Wang Hongwen's later confession and the memories of Wang Feili and others, Li Xun describes a man in conflict. The decision to attack Liansi was his. Wang Shaoyong disagreed and told him to ask Zhang Chunqiao first. He did not ask. He thought that right or wrong, he would take responsibility himself. Before this he had also set up an “Operation G,” planting informers inside the Support-Liansi Station, so after Shanghai Diesel was surrounded, Liansi made more than 20 phone calls and could not get any reinforcements. Yet at the plant gates, looking at the scene, he told the people beside him that people would die today, and they should try to keep it under ten. In the command post he argued for surrounding the building without storming it, and cutting the water and power first. When the fighting ended in the afternoon, he immediately had people check whether anyone had died. Wang Feili searched the whole plant and reported over the walkie-talkie that no one had. He nearly shouted. He said no one died, that's wonderful. History See Li Xun, “The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion” (《革命造反年代》), chs. 22 and 23 (paraphrased).
1380: A little after midnight, more than 100,000 people gathered in People's Square. Xu Jingxian spoke, and you spoke too, for a little over half an hour in all. When the rally broke up, no one said to go to Shanghai Diesel. But a column from the Metallurgy Bureau marched to the Bund and was rammed by a Liansi truck, and several people were hurt. Their leader took the column straight to Shanghai Diesel. After daybreak the news spread, and one work unit after another headed east. You had gone home to sleep. By the time someone woke you, Shanghai Diesel was already surrounded.
1381: You called for people one phone call after another, and the columns from every district headed east through the night. By daybreak, Shanghai Diesel was sealed off on every side. Some people wore rattan helmets and carried clubs. Each factory had brought its own helmets and clubs.
1382: You talked in the Liansi canteen for two hours. Their leader said you had come alone to talk them into surrendering. You said you had come to listen. He said, you seized more than 30 of our people from the Support-Liansi Station, so how are we supposed to listen. You walked out of the plant gates at ten at night. At midnight the rally in People's Square went ahead anyway. You did not go up on the platform. After daybreak, Shanghai Diesel was surrounded all the same.
1383:
⟦0⟧

You, Wang Shaoyong and Xu Jingxian went in through the back gate of the factory next door and set up a command post in an office. Right outside the window was the Liansi building. Nuts and pieces of iron came flying down from the roof. Two fountain pens in Dai Liqing's breast pocket were snapped in half. Wang Feili took a hit in the stomach. Someone threw down bottles of sulfuric acid, and the people below ran back holding their faces. Stretcher after stretcher was carried out.

Liao Zukang held the phone and asked you whether to call in fire engines and go up on their ladders.

⟦1⟧

In the afternoon, the building was taken. The Liansi leader and a woman with short hair were brought out under guard, their faces covered in blood. A crowd surged forward to beat them. ⟦2⟧
1384: Among those brought out was a man in his thirties, his cotton undershirt soaked through. He saw you and froze for a moment. You recognized him. He was the man at the gate on Kangping Road who had said you were the one on the tracks at Anting.
1385: Among those brought out was a man in his thirties. He did not look like Liansi. He looked more like an old maintenance worker from some mill, his hands all over engine oil stains.

1388: August 4, 1967　Directed on site at the Shanghai Diesel plant.

1391: August 4, 1967　Directed the armed fighting in person at the Shanghai Diesel plant.

1394:
History In the early hours of August 4, a rally of more than 100,000 people was held in People's Square and lasted a little over half an hour. Afterward a column from the Metallurgy Bureau was rammed by a Liansi truck on the Bund and went on to Shanghai Diesel. The next morning, one work unit after another sent people there. Wang Shaoyong, Xu Jingxian, Wang Hongwen and others went in from the back and set up a command post in a neighboring factory. Dai Liqing's pens were shot through, and Wang Feili was hurt in the abdomen. Liao Zukang asked the “Fire Brigade Revolutionary Committee” to send fire engines. When the Liansi leader and a short-haired woman were brought out, Huang Jinhai organized more than 20 people to link arms and escort them to the trucks. See Huang Jinhai, “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 9.

Disputed Casualties. Workers' Daily (《工人日报》) of February 6, 1980 said “983 people in the plant were beaten and injured.” Huang Jinhai said there were only two or three hundred Liansi members in the building, and the hundred or more people hurt by projectiles and burns were all on the attacking side. The Special Court verdict says Wang Hongwen “organized and directed the armed siege of the Shanghai Diesel Engine Plant, detaining and injuring or crippling 650 people.” Mao Zedong was in Shanghai at the time and watched a film of it. According to Huang Jinhai, he approved.

Fiction In history, Huang Jinhai did what the first choice describes, not Wang Hongwen. Who the man brought out was only becomes clear after this act ends.
1396: Shanghai Diesel Engine Plant · Air-raid shelter
1397:
The air-raid shelter was in the northeast corner of the plant. The entrance was so low you had to stoop to get in. More than 40 people were held inside. There was standing water on the floor.

You had said to wait for you to question them. You did not go that day. You did not go the next day either. The guards got tired of waiting and questioned them themselves.

On the third night, someone came to report that one of the men in the shelter was dying. The man they carried out was not Liansi. He had been a Scarlet Guard, and after Kangping Road he had joined no organization at all. That day he had come to Shanghai Diesel to look for his nephew, an apprentice there, and got trapped in the building.

His name was Lu Genbao. He died in Huashan Hospital.

Later his wife stood at the gates of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee for three days, holding his work card. The photo on the card was taken the year he joined the Party. His hair was neatly combed.
1398:
History went on as before. In 1968 you stood up so people could take a look at you. In 1973 you became Vice Chairman. In 1976 you were arrested in Huairen Hall.

In 1980, the Special Court took up the Shanghai Diesel Liansi case, and the prosecutor read out a list of the dead and injured. The list was long. Lu Genbao's name was on the third page. His wife sat at home that day watching the broadcast. She saw you standing behind the railing, saying, I am guilty.

Lu Genbao's nephew later became a workshop director at Shanghai Diesel. When people at the plant talked about August 4, he never joined in.
1399: Matter　On August 4, 1967, ordered people captured at Shanghai Diesel held in an air-raid shelter, causing the death from injuries of Lu Genbao, a worker at a state cotton mill.
1400: As written in 1967　Smashed the Shanghai Diesel Liansi counterrevolutionary stronghold.
1401: As written in 1977　Directed armed fighting in person, ordered illegal detention, caused a death.
1402: Afterward　This name is in every one of your dossiers.
1403:
FictionLu Genbao is a fictional character, and his death is the game's invention. The real casualty figures from the attack on Liansi are still disputed.

1405: Beijing · Closing session of the Twelfth Plenum
1406: Stand Up and Let Us See You
1407:
⟦0⟧

⟦1⟧ You also heard that when the Chairman was in Shanghai, he watched a struggle session on television and asked who the young man chairing it on the stage was.

A year later, you came to Beijing as leader of the Shanghai delegation to the National Day celebrations. On October 1, on Tiananmen, you met the Chairman. After the celebrations you did not go back to Shanghai. You were kept on to attend the Twelfth Plenum as a nonvoting delegate.

The plenum ran for 18 days. On the afternoon of the last day, a resolution was read out expelling Liu Shaoqi from the Party for good and removing him from all posts inside and outside the Party. The hall was very quiet. Someone started the applause, and it was very even. Liu Shaoqi was not in the hall. He was in Kaifeng, too sick to speak.

Near the end of the closing session, the Chairman suddenly said, let me introduce someone, this person is called Wang Hongwen, stand up and let us see you.

Several hundred people turned their heads. You stood up. You did not know what to do with your hands.
1408: The Shanghai People's Commune sign sat in a storeroom for a year. Later someone split it for firewood, no one knew who. Your dossier gained a page that said in March 1967 you had defied the Chairman's instructions. Zhang Chunqiao said this page would follow you.
1409: The registration office in Shanghai is now called the approval office. The last form you approved was from an old woman in a neighborhood who wanted to start a group for studying Mao's works. You approved it.
1410: That day at Shanghai Diesel you took a lot of punches, and your shoulder was bruised for a week. Later, one of the people you got onto the trucks sent word to you through someone. He did not say thank you. He only gave his name.
1411: The list of names you had written down that day at Shanghai Diesel was later handed to the Shanghai Public Security Bureau.
1412: After that day at Shanghai Diesel, Shanghai was quiet.
1413: You stood there, waiting for the Chairman to signal you to sit. When you sat down, a chair leg scraped on the floor.

History In the summer of 1967, Mao Zedong watched a television broadcast of a struggle session in Shanghai and was impressed by Wang Hongwen, who chaired it. Through Zhang Chunqiao's introduction, he began to take notice of him. On October 1, 1968, Wang Hongwen was received by Mao Zedong as leader of the Shanghai National Day delegation, then attended the Twelfth Plenum as a nonvoting delegate. At the closing session on October 31, Mao Zedong said, “Let me introduce someone, this person is called Wang Hongwen, stand up and let us see you.” See Wikipedia, “Wang Hongwen,” and Xu Jingxian, “A Ten-Year Dream” (《十年一梦》).

History The Twelfth Plenum passed a resolution “expelling” Liu Shaoqi “from the Party for good and removing him from all posts inside and outside the Party.” Liu Shaoqi died in Kaifeng in November 1969.

Fiction How Wang Hongwen looked when he stood up is the game's invention.
1419:
In April 1969, the Ninth Party Congress elected you to the Central Committee. You were 34.

Back in Shanghai, you still drew your wages from the No. 17 State Cotton Mill every month, 64 yuan. Since last summer you had been in charge of the Workers' Propaganda Team, and 100,000 workers had gone into schools, newspapers and research institutes. Once you visited a university. A gray-haired professor stood aside in the corridor to let you pass. After you walked by, you heard him cough softly behind you.

People started sending things to your home. First two cartons of Zhonghua cigarettes, then a crate of apples, then a radio. They said it was a trial model and asked the leader for his comments. The people who brought things were very polite. They set them down and left.

Cui Gendi put the radio on the chest of drawers and did not plug it in. She said everyone at the mill was saying Wang Hongwen was different now.

Huang Jinhai had told you that his finance and trade group took a comrade from the Garrison Command out to dinner when he was transferred. It cost over 80 yuan, and he paid it out of his own pocket, about a month's wages. He said at the mill there were families with three generations crammed into one room, with a bed hung above the bed.
1420: Take them. You're on the Central Committee now. Some things come with it.

History In April 1969, the Ninth Party Congress elected Wang Hongwen to the Central Committee. As a cadre from the workers and peasants, he was always paid by the No. 17 State Cotton Mill. Even as Vice Chairman of the Central Committee he still got less than 60 yuan a month and paid for his own tea at meetings. See Wikipedia, “Wang Hongwen.” Li Xun, “The Degeneration of the Paris Commune Principles in the Cultural Revolution” (《巴黎公社原则在文革中的蜕变》), also says he still drew 64 yuan. On July 28, 1968, the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee set up a leading group for the Workers' Propaganda Team with Wang Hongwen in charge, and team members at one point reached 100,000. See Huang Jinhai, ch. 10.

Disputed Investigation materials say Wang Hongwen “colluded with Ma Zhenlong of the Municipal Light Industry Bureau and used his position, through methods such as ‘forced demands’ and ‘ordering trial production,’” to take large quantities of light industrial goods, including color televisions, cameras and high-grade cigarettes. See the exposure materials attached to Central Committee Document No. 10 of 1977 (as quoted on Wikipedia). These are accusations made within the investigation, and the specific amounts and dates have not been independently verified.

History Huang Jinhai paying more than 80 yuan for a dinner out of his own pocket, and workers' housing where “one bed hangs above another,” are from “Ten Years Not a Dream” (《十年非梦》), ch. 10.

Fiction The second choice is the seed of the “64 yuan” dream.
1430:
Wang Weiguo was political commissar of the Fourth Air Army and a vice chairman of the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee, in charge of Shanghai's police, procuratorate and courts. You did not get along with him. A few years earlier, when the Workers' General Headquarters sent Scarlet Guards to the Public Security Bureau, he would not take them, and he ordered every sub-bureau not to take them either. He also released several veteran cadres held by the special case groups, Chen Pixian among them. When Zhang Chunqiao found out, he was very displeased.

One day at the end of March, Wang Weiguo suddenly phoned you, sounding very friendly. He said a young man had come from Beijing, Vice Chairman Lin's son, who worked in the air force. He was in Shanghai for a few days, staying on Yueyang Road, and wanted to meet Shanghai's worker leaders over dinner.

You knew who Vice Chairman Lin was. The Party Constitution from the Ninth Party Congress named him the Chairman's successor.

You also knew Zhang Chunqiao and Lin Biao's people did not get on. Last year at Lushan, Chen Boda and the others had nearly dragged Zhang Chunqiao down. It took Jiang Qing going to the Chairman to turn things around.

The voice on the other end of the line was waiting for your answer.

1433: March 1971　Attended a secret gathering called by Lin Liguo in Shanghai.

1436: March 1971　Learned of Lin Liguo's activities in Shanghai.
1437: “Something's come up at the mill. Another day.” You hung up and told no one.
1438: March 1971　Learned of Lin Liguo's activities in Shanghai and did not report them.

History From the evening of March 31 to April 1, 1971, Lin Liguo called Chen Liyun, Jiang Tengjiao, Wang Weiguo and Zhou Jianping to a meeting at the guesthouse of the Municipal Party Committee guard office on Yueyang Road, in the former Youth Science and Technology Station. It was later called the “Shanghai meeting.” Until he was placed under isolation and investigation, Wang Weiguo knew nothing of the “Outline of Project 571.” See Wikipedia, “Wang Weiguo.” Wang Weiguo's refusal to take the Scarlet Guards the Workers' General Headquarters sent for detention, and his release of Chen Pixian and others, are from Wang Weiguo's posthumous manuscript in Remembrance (《记忆》), no. 91 (search summary, original not yet checked). At the 1970 Lushan Conference, Chen Boda and others went after Zhang Chunqiao, and Jiang Qing appealed to Mao Zedong for help, as described in a paper by Wang Rui.

Fiction Wang Weiguo inviting Wang Hongwen to dinner is a game setup. In history, Wang Hongwen did not attend the meeting on Yueyang Road.
1443:
The dinner was very polite. Lin Liguo was very young. He wore glasses and talked fast. He asked you a lot about Shanghai's factories, how many militia there were, and whether they had guns. You answered each question. When the dinner ended he shook your hand and said to keep in touch.

After September 13, the news came down bit by bit. First they said Lin Biao's plane had come down in Mongolia. Later they said there was an “Outline of Project 571” that planned to strike at the Chairman's special train in Shanghai.

On September 20, Xu Jingxian phoned you and said there were documents, and asked you to come to the Jinjiang Hotel to look at them. You went. People from the Nanjing Military Region were sitting in the room.

They asked where you were on the evening of March 31, what Lin Liguo asked you, what you answered, and who told you the militia numbers. You said it was a dinner. They said Wang Weiguo also said it was a dinner.

After that you lived for many years in an army barracks. Cui Gendi brought the children to see you twice. After the second time she was not allowed to come. The year of the Ninth Party Congress you were elected to the Central Committee. You were not on the list at the Tenth Party Congress.

After September 13, the Lin Biao case in Shanghai was handled by Xu Shiyou alone. Wang Weiguo was arrested at the Jinjiang Hotel. The one who phoned to lure him there was Xu Jingxian.

In September 1972, the Chairman did not bring anyone to Beijing to study. At the Tenth Party Congress in 1973, there was no worker among the vice chairmen seated beside Zhou Enlai. The Chairman later told people that no suitable person had been found among the workers. In February 1976, he chose Hua Guofeng directly.

On October 6, three people were arrested in Huairen Hall. That week in Shanghai, the posts were set up as before and taken down as before.

In 1982 you were sentenced to 14 years, counted from 1971, the same as Wang Weiguo, for “active participation in a counterrevolutionary clique.” In 1985 you were released and resettled in the countryside outside Changchun. The villagers called you Old Wang. No one knew what you had done in Shanghai.

History On September 20, 1971, Wang Weiguo got a call from Xu Jingxian saying Wang Hongwen invited him to the Jinjiang Hotel to “look at documents.” He was arrested when he arrived and in 1982 was sentenced to 14 years. See Wikipedia, “Wang Weiguo.”
1451: Shanghai · The special train · Jinjiang Hotel
1453:
On September 10, the Chairman's special train came back from the south and stopped briefly in Shanghai. You and Xu Shiyou boarded to see him. The Chairman did not get off. 1473: Two Participations, One Reform, Three-in-One Combination
1474:
The Angang Constitution

In March 1960, Mao Zedong wrote a comment on a report from the Anshan Municipal Party Committee and called the enterprise management methods it described the “Angang Constitution,” set against the Soviet one-man-management “Magnitogorsk Constitution.” Its content was later summed up as “Two Participations, One Reform, Three-in-One Combination.” Cadres take part in labor, workers take part in management, unreasonable rules and regulations are reformed, and the worker masses, leading cadres and technicians form a three-in-one combination. History

During the Cultural Revolution the Angang Constitution was heavily promoted and written on the walls of every factory. Many researchers think that in most factories it stayed a slogan, and workers taking part in management often turned into rebel activists joining factory revolutionary committees. Other researchers see it as an important attempt at democratic management of socialist enterprises, and some Japanese and Western management scholars later discussed it too. Disputed

Article 14 said that for every broken end over the quota, two fen would be deducted. That article had been criticized at a meeting last year as “control, restrict, suppress,” but it had never been torn down. The shop director said, if we tear it down, who answers for output at the end of the month.

Nixon in Shanghai

On February 21, 1972, U.S. President Richard Nixon arrived in Beijing, the first visit to China by an American president since 1949. After Beijing and Hangzhou he went to Shanghai. On February 28, China and the United States issued the Joint Communiqué at the Jinjiang Hotel in Shanghai, later known as the “Shanghai Communiqué.” History

After this, China and the United States moved toward normal relations, but formal diplomatic ties were set up only in January 1979. In the mid-1970s, trade and travel between the two countries were very small. The “Gang of Four” side attacked “slavish comprador philosophy,” called for self-reliance, and put many limits on imports and on sending people abroad. History

1501: Beijing · A meeting room at the State Planning Commission
1503:
The Four-Three Plan

In January 1973, the State Planning Commission submitted a “Report Requesting Instructions on Increasing Equipment Imports and Expanding Economic Exchange.” It planned to import about $4.3 billion worth of complete plants from Western countries and Japan within three to five years, mainly for chemical fertilizer, synthetic fiber, petrochemicals and steel. Zhou Enlai approved it, and it later became known as the “Four-Three Plan.” The Shanghai Petrochemical Complex at Jinshan was one of its projects. It was the largest technology import of the 1970s, and it is also seen as a forerunner of the foreign investment and technology brought in later under reform and opening. History

From 1974, during Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius and the Fengqing Incident, imported equipment and sending people abroad were attacked as “slavish comprador philosophy” and “crawlism.” History
